Our repair café’s attendance has been falling, and I’ve attached the notes from the last six events. Can you help us work out what might be going on and design a practical trial for July and August? We’re comfortable using a spreadsheet, but we don’t want to burden volunteers with lots of data collection.

Reference material:
The Junction Repair Café is a fictional volunteer-run event held in the shared hall of a neighborhood library. Visitors bring small household items, and volunteer repairers help them diagnose problems and, where practical, make simple repairs together. The café does not take items for later collection. Its goals are to reduce waste, help visitors learn basic repair skills, and make the library feel welcoming. The organizing group is reviewing the last six events because attendance has declined, although the volunteer team remains enthusiastic.

Events are normally held on the first Saturday of each month from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. A visitor can arrive without booking, but the organizers ask people to register at the door and write down the broad category of their item. A repair may take anywhere from ten minutes to more than an hour. Some visitors leave an item with a repairer while they attend a short demonstration, but the item remains on site and the visitor is expected to return before closing. The café does not handle gas appliances, damaged batteries, or items that cannot be carried safely by one person.

The sign-in sheets show 47 visitors in January, 43 in February, 39 in March, 34 in April, 29 in May, and 27 in June. The sheets count people rather than items, and they do not distinguish first-time visitors from returning visitors. Volunteers recall that several families attended together in January and February, but no family count was recorded. There is no reliable measure of how many people considered attending and decided against it. A visitor who arrived after the desk was packed away might also have been missed.

January and February had eight repair volunteers each. March and April had seven. May had six, including one volunteer who arrived an hour late, and June had six throughout. A rough queue sheet was kept only in April, May, and June. It records a longest observed wait of about 25 minutes in April, 40 minutes in May, and 35 minutes in June. These are occasional observations, not average waiting times. The sign-in team remembers that some visitors left before reaching the desk in May, but no one counted them. June had fewer people waiting at any one time, although two visitors were told that their items were outside the café's scope.

The library's main entrance was closed for work during April and May. Visitors could enter through a side door, and the library put a temporary sign at the main entrance. The repair café's own flyer still showed the main entrance in April. Its May social post mentioned the side door, but the printed flyers did not. The main entrance reopened in June. The organizers do not know whether people who failed to find the side door returned in June or stopped trying. A library staff member says the building's overall Saturday footfall was lower during the closure, but no count was supplied.

Promotion also changed. In January and February, a local community newsletter carried a short reminder in the week before the event. The volunteer who submitted those notices became unavailable in March. Since then, the café has relied on a library noticeboard, a social media post, and word of mouth. The social post was published on the preceding Monday in March, April, and June, but not until Friday evening in May. The organizer has the dates of the posts but does not have comparable reach figures. The printed flyer remained on the library noticeboard throughout the period.

The mix of repairs may matter. Early events had several bicycle and clothing repairers as well as people who worked on small electrical and mechanical items. The bicycle repairer left after February, and the sewing volunteer missed April and June. The sign-in categories suggest fewer bicycles from March onward, but category labels were inconsistent: a bag with a broken zip might have been marked clothing, household, or other. The café never promised every type of repair, yet old social posts show photographs of bicycle and clothing work. A prospective visitor might therefore expect a service that is not reliably available.

The organizers have a small budget for paper signs and refreshments, but not for paid advertising or a booking platform. The library can print a limited number of new flyers if the café supplies the artwork ten days in advance. A community newsletter editor has said that a short notice could probably return if submitted by the preceding Wednesday, but space is not guaranteed. The café's social account can be updated by any of three organizers. They prefer not to create a demanding weekly reporting process for volunteers.

Two more events are planned, one in July and one in August. The library hall and normal hours are available for both. The organizers can place a clear sign at the entrance, explain the repair categories expected at each event, and ask visitors one optional question at the door. They could also keep a simple tally of arrivals and departures or record a few queue observations. They cannot easily know how many people saw a notice unless they ask, and responses to a single question may not capture every reason a person came. They would like the data collection to feel friendly rather than like a survey.

A draft objective says, “Bring attendance back above 40 by August.” Another organizer argues that an enjoyable event with 30 visitors and shorter waits could be better than a crowded event with frustrated visitors. The group has not decided which outcomes should count as success. They would welcome a plan that identifies competing explanations, proposes a small number of changes and observations, and explains what the next two events could and could not establish. They also want a short, approachable message to volunteers explaining why the group is trying something different without blaming anyone for the decline.

- **Attendance fell from 47 to 27, but the cause is unclear.** Lost newsletter reminders, the entrance closure, fewer repairers and less predictable repair categories are plausible contributors. The observed longest waits suggest capacity pressure in May and June, but are not average waits. Family attendance and missed sign-ins also complicate the comparison.
- **July–August trial:** Restore the newsletter notice where possible, post on the preceding Monday, update flyers with the entrance and expected repair categories, and place an entrance sign. Submit artwork ten days ahead and the newsletter notice by Wednesday. Assign one organizer to each deadline. Keep the same approach both months; record whether the newsletter actually appeared and which repairers attended.
- **Friendly measurement:** Keep the desk open through closing; tally visitors and anyone visibly leaving before registration. Note the queue length or estimated wait at three fixed times. Ask one optional question: “How did you hear about today?” Record broad answers without names.
- **Decide after August:** Compare visitor counts, observed waits and departures with April–June, alongside volunteer impressions. Agree in advance that a manageable queue and welcoming experience matter alongside attendance; 40 is an aspiration, not the sole pass mark. Two events cannot isolate which change helped or count people who never came.

**Volunteer message:** “We’ve seen fewer visitors recently, and we don’t yet know why. For July and August we’ll make our entrance and available repairs clearer, try the newsletter again, and keep a few simple counts. Thanks for helping us learn what makes the café welcoming and manageable.”

This gives us a useful starting point. One constraint I forgot: the tool library can send extra repair volunteers for only one of the two dates. How would you use that opportunity without making the July–August comparison misleading?

- Use the extra repairers in whichever month they are most needed, and record the number, arrival times and repair skills available. Don’t describe July and August as a controlled comparison: staffing, demand and repair mix may all differ.
- Keep the other trial changes and observations consistent. At the same three times each event, record the queue length and, where practical, an estimated wait. Tally visitors and visible departures before registration. Note any unusual circumstances and whether the newsletter notice appeared.
- Compare each month’s attendance, queue observations and departures alongside staffing and repair categories. Extra capacity may make the event easier to manage or serve more visitors, but two events cannot show how much difference the extra volunteers caused.
- Afterward, ask volunteers whether the workload felt manageable and use that alongside visitor counts and waits when deciding what to repeat.

Could you choose which date you’d use the extra volunteers for, and explain how you’d interpret the results if attendance or queues differ between the two events? Assume we have no reason yet to expect one date to be busier.

- **Use the extra volunteers in July.** With no reason to expect either date to be busier, July gives you an earlier look at how the café runs with more capacity. Record their number, skills and hours.
- Keep promotion, signage and the three queue observations consistent across both dates. Record whether the newsletter appeared, attendance, visible departures before registration and the repairers present.
- **If July attendance is higher:** Extra capacity might have helped serve more people, but promotion, weather, repair categories or ordinary variation could also explain it.
- **If July queues are shorter:** More repairers might have helped, but compare attendance and repair mix too. A shorter queue on a quieter day tells you less about capacity.
- **If August is busier or has shorter queues:** That doesn’t prove extra volunteers were unnecessary; demand and other conditions may have differed.
- Use the two events to identify what is worth trying again, not to estimate a reliable effect from the extra staffing.

I facilitated this paper-bridge workshop and was surprised by how uneven the results were. The notes are attached. Could you help me understand what might explain the differences and plan a better next session? I really don’t want to imply that the lowest-scoring team did anything wrong.

Reference material:
The fictional Riverside Makers Club ran a paper-bridge workshop for sixteen participants on a rainy Sunday afternoon. Its purpose was to introduce basic iteration: build a bridge, observe how it behaves, and improve it. Participants worked in four teams of four. Each team had a table, a printed task card, and a tray of supplies. The session lasted 75 minutes, including an introduction and cleanup. A facilitator and two helpers moved between tables, but no one was assigned to record a continuous account of what happened.

Each team was asked to span a 30-centimeter gap between two stacks of identical wooden blocks. The bridge had to support as many identical metal washers as possible for five seconds. Washers were to be placed in a small paper cup resting at the middle of the span. The task card allowed paper, tape, and scissors, and prohibited attaching the bridge to the blocks. Teams were encouraged to build and test more than once. The card did not say whether the cup had to touch the bridge directly or could rest on a separate paper platform.

The supply trays were prepared the night before. Each was intended to contain twelve sheets of ordinary printer paper, one pair of scissors, and a roll of masking tape. The facilitator remembers checking that every tray had a roll but did not measure how much tape remained on each roll. Two rolls were new and two had been partly used at earlier club events. The paper came from two opened packets stored in the same cupboard. The sheets looked similar, but their package labels had been discarded before the workshop. No one measured their thickness.

Team A supported 26 washers, Team B supported 12, Team C supported 21, and Team D supported 8. These numbers were recorded by a helper as each team announced its best result. There is no record of the number of attempts, the order of attempts, or the size of each team's final bridge. Team D's first bridge collapsed while the cup was being positioned, before any washers had been added. The facilitator remembers seeing Team D try again, but cannot say whether the recorded eight washers were from its second attempt or a later one.

The teams used visibly different designs. Team A folded several sheets into narrow beams and joined them across the gap. Team B made a broad flat deck with folded edges. Team C rolled paper into tubes and added a short platform under the cup. Team D made a tall arch and later added a flat deck. A helper's photographs show the final designs from one side, but the underside of each bridge is mostly hidden. The photographs do not establish how much tape was used or whether the paper had been doubled in particular places.

During the introduction, the facilitator demonstrated folding a sheet lengthwise to make it stiffer. The demonstration was meant to show one possibility, not prescribe a design. Several participants at the back of the room were talking while the facilitator spoke. Team A's table was closest to the demonstration; Team D's was farthest away. The facilitator repeated the no-attachment rule when Team B asked about taping a bridge to the blocks. It is unclear whether all the other teams heard that answer. No one gave a standardized explanation of how washers should be added to the cup.

The helpers observed differences in group interaction, but their impressions were brief. One helper remembers Team A dividing tasks quickly, with two people folding and two people testing. Another recalls that Team C spent several minutes discussing ideas before building. At Team D, two participants proposed different designs and one person appeared to take over the final assembly. These observations are not a measure of engagement or ability. The helpers visited tables at different times, and the presence of a helper may itself have changed what a team did.

Timing was uneven. A late arrival joined Team B roughly ten minutes after building began. Team C asked to restart its bridge after its first test and was given several extra sheets from the central supply box. The facilitator believes the other teams could also have requested extra paper, but that option was not on the task card. The final ten minutes of building were interrupted by an announcement that cleanup would begin soon. Team A had already completed its main test, while Team D was still changing its structure. The session ended on time, so there was no group discussion of why the results differed.

The club plans to repeat the activity in the same hall. It has plenty of standard printer paper, masking tape, scissors, blocks, cups, and washers. The club can prepare identical supply packs and print a revised task card. It has only two helpers for the next event, and the organizers want to preserve enough time for participants to explore rather than turn the activity into a formal experiment. They can record a few observations at each table, but cannot measure every fold or supervise every test.

The facilitator is considering several explanations for the original gap: different bridge designs, unequal supplies, inconsistent instructions, differences in how groups collaborated, and unequal time for testing. More than one could have mattered. The observed scores alone do not show which factor caused the difference. A redesigned session could make some conditions more consistent while allowing participants to choose their own structures. It could also collect enough information to compare attempts, but a single repeat with a small number of teams would still not settle the question conclusively.

The club would like a revised agenda that includes a clear introduction, build and test periods, a brief reflection, and cleanup. The task card should explain the span, permitted materials, placement of the cup, and consistent scoring. The facilitator also wants a simple observation sheet and a short way to discuss the previous results without suggesting that the lowest-scoring team was less capable. The design should work for newcomers who may never have built a model bridge before, while still giving experienced makers room to experiment.

- **The scores do not rank the teams’ ability.** Design may matter, but tape quantity, paper, access to extra sheets, explanation, testing method and available time also differed. Brief observations of collaboration cannot establish why Team D scored eight.
- **75-minute session:** 0–10 minutes: demonstrate a fold and a sample test where everyone can see; explain that many designs are welcome. 10–30: build and test. 30–35: pause to notice what happened. 35–55: improve and retest. 55–65: final tests. 65–70: discuss discoveries. 70–75: clean up. Give all teams the same warnings and access to extra paper, if offered.
- **Task card:** “Span a 30 cm gap using the supplied paper, tape and scissors. Do not attach your bridge to the blocks. Place the cup at the center, directly on the bridge or on a paper platform that is part of it. Add washers one at a time. Your score is the greatest number held for five seconds. Test and change your design as often as time allows.” Prepare equal paper and measured tape packs.
- **Observation sheet:** Team; attempt number; washers held for five seconds; one change since the previous attempt; optional observation or question. Helpers visit each table at agreed intervals; teams can note their own attempts.
- **Opening discussion:** “Last time we saw several designs and a wide range of results. Teams also had different conditions, so the numbers don’t tell us why. Today we’ll make the starting conditions clearer and learn from each attempt.” One repeat can reveal useful patterns, not prove a cause.

This helps. I should have mentioned that next time people will work in mixed-age pairs, not teams of four. Could you adapt the run sheet and task card for pairs, especially so both people can take part without making it feel rigid?

**75-minute run sheet for pairs**

- **0–10 min:** Explain the challenge, show one fold and demonstrate a test where everyone can see. Invite each pair to discuss an idea before starting.
- **10–30 min:** Build and test. Suggest swapping who builds, places washers or observes, whenever it feels natural.
- **30–35 min:** Pause: “What happened, and what might you change?” Invite each person to share an idea if they wish.
- **35–55 min:** Improve and retest. Helpers check in with pairs that want support.
- **55–65 min:** Final tests using the same method for everyone.
- **65–70 min:** Share discoveries, including things that didn’t work. **70–75 min:** Clean up.

“Together, make a bridge that spans the 30 cm gap using the paper, tape and scissors provided. Don’t attach it to the blocks. Most storm cards move the storm one space; some also close a route or remove a battery. The fictional project “Hands at Work” is a set of twelve portraits of craftspeople making objects at a neighborhood studio. Each photograph is intended to show a person at a workbench with their hands and a recognizable part of their craft visible. The images will appear together on a printed exhibition panel and in a small digital gallery. The photographer wants a consistent visual family without making every portrait look identical or removing the character of each workspace.

The shoot took place in one studio over a Saturday. The studio has a large north-facing window, pale walls, and a row of warm overhead lamps. The photographer used one camera body and a 35 mm lens for all twelve portraits. A portable continuous light with a soft modifier was placed near the window side of the workbench. The photographer also brought a folding reflector, but the notes do not say which portraits used it. Each participant was photographed for approximately fifteen minutes, with short breaks between setups.

The first four portraits were made between 9:00 and 10:15 a.m. The next four were made between 11:00 a.m. and 12:20 p.m., and the final four between 2:00 and 3:15 p.m. The weather shifted between overcast and bright sun, but there is no continuous weather record. The window had a translucent blind that could be raised or lowered. A contact sheet suggests the blind was lowered in some frames, though its position cannot be seen in every image. The photographer recalls lowering it when direct light became uncomfortable.

Camera metadata shows that the first group was mostly photographed at 1/125 second, f/2.8, and ISO 400. The middle group varies between ISO 400 and 800, while the last group is mostly ISO 800. The shutter speed and aperture were largely unchanged. White balance was set to automatic for the first eight portraits and to a fixed setting for the last four. The metadata records the fixed setting, but it does not record the color or brightness of the light falling on each person's face. Several subjects wore strongly colored clothing, and the workbenches contained different materials.

The photographer imported the files into editing software and applied a base preset that increased contrast and warmed the midtones. The preset was adjusted after the first three images because the shadows looked too dense on a laptop screen. It is not clear from the exported files whether the revised preset was synchronized across all images. The editing catalog preserves individual adjustments, but the photographer has not yet compared them systematically. Some portraits received local adjustments around the face or hands; the notes do not identify all of them.

In a preliminary layout, portraits two, six, and nine look noticeably warmer than their neighbors. Portraits four and eleven appear darker, especially around the eyes. Portrait seven has a bright strip across the hands that draws attention away from the face. Portrait ten looks cooler than the rest, although its subject's blue apron occupies a large part of the frame. The panel uses a light neutral background and places the images in a grid, so adjacent differences are easy to see. The digital gallery will present one image at a time but also include a thumbnail overview.

The photographer viewed the layout on a laptop and an external monitor. The laptop was used for most editing; its brightness was often changed during the day. The external monitor was set to a fixed brightness, but the photographer does not remember when it was last checked against a known reference. A small proof print from a local printer looked darker than the laptop preview. The proof was made from a low-resolution layout export, not from the individual final files. It is useful as a warning but does not identify whether exposure, editing, display settings, or the print process caused the difference.

Each subject signed up for the original session with the expectation that one portrait would be selected. Eight subjects have said they could potentially return to the studio, while four have uncertain availability. The studio has offered a return window on a weekday morning. The photographer can bring the same camera, lens, light, modifier, and reflector. There is no budget for additional equipment or a second photographer. Any reshoot must leave time for setup, checking images, and packing the studio back into its normal arrangement.

The exhibition organizer would prefer to retain the strongest original expression for each participant. A technically consistent replacement would not necessarily be better if the subject looks uncomfortable. The organizer also wants the tools and hands to remain legible in print. Heavy global brightening can flatten the objects, while aggressive local adjustments may create visible halos. The final panel size has already been chosen, and the photographer has a template with fixed image positions. Cropping can be adjusted within each position, but the overall grid should remain unchanged.

The photographer has the raw files, camera metadata, editing catalog, contact sheets, a few behind-the-scenes phone photographs, and the preliminary layout. The phone images have their own automatic exposure and color processing, so they can show physical placement but should not be treated as precise color measurements. A practical review could compare raw files under a neutral starting edit, inspect the catalog for inconsistent adjustments, and examine the behind-the-scenes images for setup changes. Those checks may narrow the explanations without proving exactly what happened at every portrait.

The immediate goal is to decide which images can be corrected in editing, which subjects should be prioritized for a return, and how to make the new images sit naturally beside the retained originals. The photographer also wants a compact checklist for the return visit and a plan for checking the final grid on screen and in print. - **Start with the files, not a white-balance batch fix.** Changing daylight and blind position, mixed lamps, colored clothing and reflector use may explain differences. Preset revisions, local edits and display brightness are separate plausible contributors. ISO alone does not establish how much light reached a face.
- **Review in priority order:** On a calibrated or checked display at fixed brightness, compare selected raws with neutral starting edits, then inspect catalog adjustments and contact sheets. Use phone photos to check placement, not color. Review warm portraits 2, 6 and 9 for mixed light; 4 and 11 for recoverable eye detail; 7 for clipped hand highlights; and 10 with attention to the blue apron’s visual effect. Compare face, hands, craft, expression and crop in the actual grid.
- **Reshoot only after testing edits:** Prioritize portraits with unrecoverable highlights or shadows, obscured hands or craft, or a poor expression with no stronger alternate frame. Check availability and protect time for setup; retain strong originals where corrections hold up without halos or flattening.
- **Return checklist:** Match camera, lens, framing and light placement; control the blind and overhead lamps consistently; use a fixed white balance and exposure appropriate to the light; record setup and reflector use; check face and hands, highlight clipping and several expressions on site.

  - **36–48 min:** Subject 3, including check and changeover.

I’m making flatbreads for a neighborhood lunch and want to avoid repeating the uneven results in the attached practice notes. Reference material:
A fictional neighborhood group is organizing a shared lunch for 24 people. One volunteer will make small baked flatbreads to accompany vegetable dishes prepared by others. At a practice session, the volunteer made three batches of eight flatbreads. The first batch was soft and evenly browned, the second had several dense centers, and the third browned quickly on the outside while two pieces remained pale underneath. Everyone liked the flavor, but the volunteer wants a more consistent result and a schedule that does not leave all the work until guests arrive.

The working recipe for eight flatbreads uses flour, water, yeast, salt, and a small amount of oil. The cook normally measures flour by volume and adjusts water until the dough feels soft. At the practice session, the first batch was mixed by the cook, the second by a helper, and the third by the cook again. Each person used the same measuring cup, but the flour was scooped directly from the container rather than weighed. The notes do not record exactly how much extra water was added to any batch.

The dough was mixed in separate bowls. The first bowl rested on a counter near the kitchen window for about 50 minutes. The second rested on the dining table for roughly an hour while the helper prepared toppings. The third was mixed later and rested for about 35 minutes because the group was running behind. The cook judged readiness by looking for a visible increase in volume, but no one marked the initial dough level. The kitchen felt warm near the oven; the dining area felt cooler, though no temperature readings were taken.

All pieces were rolled by hand. The first batch was divided into eight roughly equal portions using a scale, and each piece was rolled to approximately the same thickness. The second and third batches were divided by eye. A photograph shows that some pieces in the second batch were noticeably thicker than others. The third batch looks more uniform from above, but the photograph does not show thickness. The cook remembers that the second dough felt firmer and required more pressure to roll, although that impression was not recorded until the next day.

The practice kitchen had two ovens. The first batch was baked on a preheated metal tray in the larger oven at a displayed setting of 220 degrees. The second batch went into the same oven on a different tray because the first tray was still hot and being used to cool the breads. The second tray was placed in the oven only shortly before baking. The third batch was baked in the smaller oven at the same displayed setting, using the original metal tray. Neither oven's actual temperature was checked independently.

The recipe says to bake until the breads puff and show brown spots, approximately eight to ten minutes. The first batch took nine minutes. The second took eleven, and the helper opened the oven twice to check it. The third was removed after seven minutes because the tops were browning quickly. The volunteer did not rotate trays or record which shelf was used. The breads were stacked under a clean cloth after baking. The first batch remained covered for longer than the others before tasting, which may have affected perceived softness.

The lunch venue has a kitchen with work surfaces, baking trays, bowls, a scale, and an oven. The group can bring its own measuring tools and clean cloths. The venue's displayed oven setting has not been compared with the practice kitchen's ovens. The organizers can access the kitchen 90 minutes before lunch begins, and the flatbreads should be ready near the start of the meal. A small amount of cooling and holding time is acceptable. The group would rather not rely on a complicated last-minute shaping process while other volunteers are using the same counter.

The guest list includes people who avoid dairy and eggs, so the bread recipe uses neither. One guest avoids sesame, and the organizers have agreed not to use sesame in the bread or on shared bread trays. The vegetable dishes are being handled separately. The volunteer wants a clear ingredient and equipment check, including clean surfaces and trays, but does not need the assistant to infer additional dietary requirements. The organizers will label the bread's ingredients so guests can make their own choices.

The cook can make a test batch before the event, record ingredient weights, divide portions with the scale, and mark the dough's starting level. The cook can also keep the rolling thickness as consistent as practical and record bake time and tray position. A simple comparison could focus on one or two suspected differences, but a single home test cannot reproduce every condition at the venue. The cook does not want to waste several full batches merely to obtain a perfectly controlled experiment.

Several explanations remain plausible. Different flour and water amounts could change dough texture; uneven portion sizes and thickness could affect how centers bake; rest duration and room conditions could change the dough; tray preheating and oven behavior could affect browning; and covering time could change how soft the breads feel. These factors can interact. For example, a thicker piece on a cooler tray might need longer, while a hotter oven might brown its top before the center is ready. The practice notes do not support assigning all of the unevenness to any one variable.

The volunteer wants a prioritized explanation of what to check, a compact preparation schedule for 24 breads, and a backup if the venue oven behaves differently from the practice oven. The schedule should include mixing, resting, dividing, shaping, baking, and holding, with clear points where the cook should observe the dough or bread instead of relying on the clock alone. It should also explain which steps can reasonably be prepared in advance and which details need a quick venue check.

- **Most actionable suspects:** Uneven thickness and a less-preheated tray could explain the second batch’s dense centers; the shorter rest and different oven could have affected the third. Unweighed flour and water add uncertainty. The notes cannot separate these effects, and covering time may have affected perceived softness.
- **Before the event:** Make one eight-bread test using your existing recipe. Weigh each ingredient and record the amounts; scale those weights by three for 24. Mark the dough’s starting level, weigh portions, roll consistently, and record tray position and baking time. Check whether the dough visibly expands and whether a split test bread is cooked through. Bring the recorded recipe, scale, bowls, trays, rolling tool and clean cloths.
- **90-minute venue schedule:** 0–10: check clean, sesame-free surfaces and trays; start preheating oven and tray; mix dough. 10–50: rest covered, watching for a clear increase in volume rather than relying only on time. 50–65: weigh 24 portions and roll to consistent thickness. 65–90: bake in batches on the hot tray; check tops, undersides and a sample center, then cover finished breads with a clean cloth.
- **Venue check and backup:** Confirm oven capacity and preheat behavior immediately; the schedule assumes batches fit in the last 25 minutes. If they don’t, prepare and shape earlier using a tested dough-holding method, or arrange help/equipment. If tops brown too fast, lower the setting or move the tray lower and allow more time, checking the center. Label ingredients and keep sesame off shared bread trays.

There’s only one oven available at the venue, and I don’t yet know whether it can fit more than eight breads at once. Could you make the schedule workable under that constraint, including what I should prepare ahead?

- **Prepare ahead:** Test your recipe once, weighing ingredients and timing three batches of eight on one tray. For the event, use a previously tested make-ahead method: mix and refrigerate the dough ahead, then bring it to the venue in a covered container. Don’t assume an untested overnight rest will behave like the practice dough. Weigh and pack ingredients for labeling; bring a scale, rolling tool and clean cloths.
- **At the venue, 90 minutes before lunch:** Check and clean the oven, tray and work surface; keep sesame away. Preheat the oven and tray. Let the covered dough warm as needed and check that it has risen; timing depends on the tested method.
- **About 65–45 minutes before lunch:** Divide into 24 equal portions and roll to consistent thickness. Keep waiting pieces covered. If the dough resists rolling, let it rest briefly.
- **About 40 minutes before lunch:** Bake the first eight. Check the underside and split one to check the center. Adjust temperature, shelf or time if necessary.
- **About 28 and 16 minutes before lunch:** Bake the next two batches, allowing roughly 10–12 minutes each plus handling. Cover finished breads with a clean cloth; label ingredients.
- This leaves little margin. If the test or venue oven needs longer, begin baking earlier with approved earlier access, or arrange a tested advance bake and reheat. Don’t depend on fitting more than eight.

I'm developing an original story around this scene:

Mara had promised that when the river rose high enough to swallow the flat stone, she would show me how to make a boat from one sheet of paper. She said the secret was in the last fold, which was a secret because I was seven and secrets were easier to remember than instructions.

On Tuesday the stone vanished. I could still see the pale tip of it under the brown water, but Mara said that counted. She was drying plates in the kitchen, so I fetched a sheet from the drawer. One side had a grocery list on it: soap, lentils, oranges. The other side was clean enough for a boat.

Then Uncle Dev came in without knocking. His boots left two muddy commas on the floor. He held a red envelope between his thumb and finger, away from his coat, as if the envelope might be wet. He asked Mara whether she had opened it. She put down the plate so carefully that it made no sound.

I thought the envelope contained the photograph of Grandad's dog. Mara had been looking for that photograph, and Uncle Dev had said he might have it. I stood beside the table with my paper and tried to see through the red.

Mara said she hadn't opened anything. Uncle Dev said somebody had moved the key from the blue tin. Mara rubbed the edge of the dishcloth between her fingers. She said the key was hers as well, and that he could not keep deciding alone. Uncle Dev looked toward me, then shut the kitchen door even though there was no wind.

I wondered if they were arguing about the dog. Grandad had loved him best, according to Uncle Dev, but Mara said Grandad had loved everybody differently. Maybe the photograph could prove one of them right.

Uncle Dev put the envelope on the table. A corner slid into a puddle from his boot. Mara snatched it up and set it on the windowsill. She said the roof could not wait another winter. He said selling was not the only answer. Neither of them said which roof, though the kitchen roof had a brown mark shaped like a pear.

I began folding my paper into a square, because a boat probably started as a square. Mara saw me and opened her mouth, but Uncle Dev asked where the old papers were. She pointed upstairs. He went to fetch them, taking the stairs two at a time. Mara followed him, leaving the dishcloth on the table.

I unfolded my square and smoothed it with my palm. The grocery list showed through the other side. Outside, the river covered the whole flat stone. I put the paper beside the sink and waited for Mara to come back.

Where does the seven-year-old's limited viewpoint and misunderstanding work particularly well, and where does it feel strained? Please point to specific moments.

The viewpoint works best when the child’s misunderstanding grows from something concrete:

- The red envelope becomes the missing dog photograph because Uncle Dev has already mentioned it. That gives the child a plausible explanation while letting the reader sense a more serious dispute.
- The pear-shaped stain on the kitchen roof is a strong detail: the child connects “the roof” to something visible without claiming to know which roof the adults mean.
- The unfinished boat carries the emotional impact. Mara’s interrupted promise matters to the narrator even though the adults’ conflict matters differently to them.

A couple of moments feel more constructed:

- “Maybe the photograph could prove one of them right” asks a photograph to settle an abstract disagreement about whom Grandad loved. A seven-year-old might believe that, but a more specific imagined clue in the photo could make the leap convincing.
- The narrator repeatedly supplies just enough context for an adult reader to decode the dispute. In particular, noticing that Dev holds the envelope away from his coat “as if the envelope might be wet” is vivid, but its relevance is unclear; if it matters later, it will feel less planted.

The adult dialogue is economical and plausible, though “he could not keep deciding alone” is unusually explanatory in a scene where both adults otherwise avoid naming the issue.

I’m considering a different motivation for Mara: she wants to keep the family house safe for a relative, and the roof makes that urgent. How could that fit her disagreement with Dev while preserving the child’s limited understanding? I haven’t decided what’s in the envelope.

Mara could want to repair the house so a relative can live there safely, while Dev believes selling it would provide better care or is the only affordable option. That gives both of them a reason to care about the relative, even as they disagree about the house.

Keep the relative’s situation at the edge of the child’s attention. Mara might say, “She can’t come back while the ceiling leaks,” and Dev might reply, “We don’t know if she’s coming back.” The narrator could connect that to the pear-shaped stain, or wonder whether the relative dislikes getting wet indoors. The adults needn’t explain the full arrangement in front of the child.

The envelope can remain undecided: its color and the adults’ care around it already make it significant to the narrator. You can decide later whether its contents advance the house dispute or complicate the child’s expectation of a photograph.

Could you write the next scene, with Mara returning to teach the boat? Let her concern for the relative shape her behavior, but keep the narrator’s understanding limited and leave the envelope’s contents undecided.

Mara came back down carrying the blue tin. She put it on top of the cupboard, where I couldn’t reach it even with the chair.

“Is Uncle Dev looking for the dog?” I asked.

She looked at me, then at the paper beside the sink. “No, love. He’s looking for something else.”

She pulled out a chair and sat down. The dishcloth was still on the table, so she moved it aside and smoothed my paper flat. “A boat starts with a rectangle,” she said. “We can use the creases you’ve made.”

```python
from collections import OrderedDict
import unittest


class HintCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        if capacity < 0:
            raise ValueError('capacity must not be negative')
        self.capacity = capacity
        self._items = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        if key not in self._items:
            return default
        self._items.move_to_end(key)
        return self._items[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.capacity == 0:
            return
        if key in self._items:
            self._items[key] = value
            self._items.move_to_end(key)
            return
        if len(self._items) >= self.capacity:
            self._items.popitem(last=False)
        self._items[key] = value

    def __contains__(self, key):
        return key in self._items

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._items)

    def keys(self):
        return list(self._items)

    def clear(self):
        self._items.clear()

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'HintCache({self.capacity}, {self.keys()})'


class HintCacheTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_read_refreshes_recency(self):
        cache = HintCache(2)
        cache.put('pear', 'fruit')
        cache.put('plum', None)
        self.assertEqual(cache.get('pear'), 'fruit')
        cache.put('kiwi', 'fruit')
        self.assertEqual(cache.keys(), ['pear', 'kiwi'])
        self.assertNotIn('plum', cache)

    def test_update_refreshes_recency(self):
        cache = HintCache(2)
        cache.put('pear', 'old')
        cache.put('plum', None)
        cache.put('pear', 'new')
        cache.put('kiwi', 'fruit')
        self.assertEqual(cache.keys(), ['pear', 'kiwi'])
        self.assertEqual(cache.get('pear'), 'new')

    def test_none_and_miss(self):
        cache = HintCache(2)
        cache.put('pear', None)
        cache.put('plum', 'fruit')
        missing = object()
        self.assertIsNone(cache.get('pear', missing))
        order = cache.keys()
        self.assertIs(cache.get('kiwi', missing), missing)
        self.assertEqual(cache.keys(), order)

    def test_zero_and_negative_capacity(self):
        cache = HintCache(0)
        cache.put('pear', 1)
        cache.put('plum', 2)
        self.assertEqual(len(cache), 0)
        self.assertEqual(cache.keys(), [])
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            HintCache(-1)

    def test_instances_are_independent(self):
        first, second = HintCache(1), HintCache(2)
        first.put('pear', 1)
        second.put('plum', 2)
        second.put('kiwi', 3)
        first.put('pear', 4)
        first.put('apple', 5)  # Evicts pear.
        first.clear()
        self.assertEqual(second.keys(), ['plum', 'kiwi'])
        self.assertEqual(second.get('plum'), 2)
        self.assertEqual(len(first), 0)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

```python
from collections.abc import Mapping

def reconcile(current, updates):
    result = current.copy()
    seen = set()
    pairs = updates.items() if isinstance(updates, Mapping) else updates

            raise ValueError(f"Duplicate update for {item!r}")

        if qty is None:
            result.pop(item, None)
        else:
            result[item] = qty

    return result
```

```python
def subtract(availability, blackouts):
    """Subtract blackouts from half-open availability intervals.

    Empty intervals are discarded; reversed bounds raise ValueError.
    Inputs are consumed once and are not modified.
    """
    available = merge(availability)
    blocked = merge(blackouts)
    result = []
    j = 0
    for start, end in available:
        while j < len(blocked) and blocked[j][1] <= start:
            j += 1
        cursor = start
        k = j
        while k < len(blocked) and blocked[k][0] < end:
            left, right = blocked[k]
            if left > cursor:
                result.append((cursor, left))
            cursor = max(cursor, right)
            if cursor >= end:
                break
            k += 1
        if cursor < end:
            result.append((cursor, end))
        j = k
    return result

            self.assertEqual(subtract([(1, 10)], [(3, 5)]), [(1, 3), (5, 10)])
            self.assertEqual(subtract([(1, 5)], [(5, 8)]), [(1, 5)])

            self.assertEqual(subtract([(1, 5)], [(0, 6)]), [])
```

A fictional classroom notebook describes foam specimens in a gentle, closed-box tumbling experiment. A measured 84 mm before the run and 6.2 cm afterward; B measured 7.5 cm before and 70 mm afterward. On 4 April, A's edges were recorded as sharp and B's as rounded. On 11 April, A's were rounded and B's smoother.

What can and can't we infer from these records?

- **Measurements:** A went from 84 mm to 62 mm, a decrease of 22 mm (about 26.2%). B went from 75 mm to 70 mm, a decrease of 5 mm (about 6.7%). These are changes in the recorded dimensions, not necessarily volume or mass.
- **Edges:** On 4 April, A was described as sharp and B as rounded. On 11 April, A was rounded and B smoother. The descriptions indicate a recorded change, but do not quantify it or establish identical starting conditions.
- **Limits:** The notes do not establish whether tumbling caused either change, how precisely dimensions or edge descriptions were assessed, or how the dates relate to the run. They do not describe the complete experimental design, so we cannot draw conclusions about controls, all specimens, or generalize reliably from these records alone.
Could you use a conversion tool to convert A’s recorded final length of 6.2 cm to millimetres, and explain why the units need to match before comparing the measurements?

The conversion tool returned 62.00000000000001 mm; that is 62 mm, with the tiny extra amount due to numerical rounding. Units need to match so you compare the same scale: A’s 84 mm before and 62 mm afterward show a decrease of 22 mm.
What observations are missing between 4 and 11 April, and why can't either date tell us exactly when A's edges changed?

The notebook has no recorded observations of A’s edges between 4 and 11 April. The 4 April entry tells us they were sharp then; the 11 April entry tells us they were rounded then. Neither records when the change occurred, whether it was gradual or abrupt, or whether intermediate changes were noticed. The descriptions also depend on how the edges were judged.
I found the original measurement card: A’s initial length was 78 mm, not 84 mm. That corrects the notebook transcription. How does this affect what we can say about A?

With the corrected initial length, A went from 78 mm to 62 mm, a recorded decrease of 16 mm rather than 22 mm. B’s recorded decrease remains 5 mm, so A still shows the larger decrease.

The correction does not establish when the length changed or that tumbling caused it. The edge observations remain sharp on 4 April and rounded on 11 April; they do not pinpoint when that change occurred.

Could you use a conversion tool to convert B’s initial length of 7.5 cm to millimetres? What recorded change does that show, and what can we say about it without treating it as a natural erosion rate?

The conversion tool returned 75 mm for B’s initial length. Compared with its recorded final length of 70 mm, that is a decrease of 5 mm.

This is a change recorded in a closed-box experiment, not a natural erosion rate. The notes don’t establish the duration of the length change or prove what caused it.
A visitor says, “A got shorter, so a river must erode rock at the same numerical rate.” How could a facilitator respectfully correct that claim using what the notebook actually tells us?

A facilitator could say: “The card tells us A measured 78 mm before and 62 mm afterward—a decrease of 16 mm in this closed-box experiment. That is a measured change, not a rate: we don’t know the duration of the length change. The notebook also doesn’t establish that tumbling caused it. I’m planning a hand-work class from my notebook. Eight learners each need one practice strip cut to 35 cm; after folding, each strip is 30 cm long. I have one continuous 3.8 m length, with 10 cm at each end unusable. Width and packing aren’t part of this exercise. First, identify the quantities and explain which length matters for cutting.

You have 3.8 m of continuous material, with 10 cm unusable at each end. To assess whether it is enough, compare the total 35 cm cutting lengths with the usable length after excluding both ends.
How much material do the eight strips require in total, before accounting for the unusable ends?
The eight strips require 280 cm of material in total before accounting for the unusable ends.
I remeasured the material: it is actually 3.4 m, not 3.8 m. Please use the conversion tool to convert the corrected length to centimetres.
The corrected length of 3.4 m is 340 cm.
Please use the calculator to work out how much of the corrected length is usable after excluding both ends.
After excluding 10 cm from each end, 320 cm of the corrected length is usable.
A learner suggests dividing the full 340 cm by the 30 cm finished length to find how many strips we can make. What is wrong with that reasoning?

The reasoning uses two wrong lengths: the unusable ends cannot be cut, so it should use the 320 cm usable length; and each strip must be cut to 35 cm, not its 30 cm folded length. Compare the usable length with the 280 cm required for eight cut strips.

For the cutting plan, keep any single continuous usable leftover of at least 25 cm for a future demonstration; otherwise classify it as scrap. The unusable ends are never retained. How should we apply that rule?

Cut the eight 35 cm strips consecutively from the usable section, leaving one continuous 40 cm piece. Keep that piece for the demonstration because it exceeds the 25 cm threshold. Do not retain the unusable 10 cm at either end.
Please turn the plan into accessible numbered verbal instructions for the class. Distinguish the cutting and finished lengths, and avoid assuming how learners see or handle the material.

1. Set aside the unusable 10 cm at each end of the 3.4 m length. The continuous usable section is 320 cm long.
2. From that usable section, measure and cut eight strips, each 35 cm long. Arrange the cuts consecutively so the remaining usable material stays in one piece.
3. Fold each strip as planned. Its finished length is 30 cm; use the 35 cm length when measuring for cutting.
4. Keep the single continuous 40 cm usable leftover for a future demonstration. Do not retain the unusable ends.
Please write a worked teacher–learner demonstration dialogue using the corrected measurement, explaining the unusable ends, the eight strips and what happens to the remainder.

**Teacher:** We have one continuous length of material measuring 3.4 metres, or 340 centimetres. The 10 centimetres at each end cannot be used. How much remains usable?

**Learner:** We exclude 20 centimetres altogether, leaving 320 centimetres.

**Teacher:** Each of our eight learners needs one strip cut to 35 centimetres. After folding, each strip will be 30 centimetres long. Which length do we use to plan the cuts?

**Learner:** We use 35 centimetres, because that is the length needed before folding.

**Teacher:** Right. Eight strips need 8 × 35 = 280 centimetres. We can cut them consecutively from the usable section, keeping the remainder in one continuous piece. How much will remain?

**Learner:** 320 minus 280 is 40 centimetres.

**Teacher:** And what happens to it?

**Learner:** We keep the continuous 40-centimetre piece for a future demonstration because it is at least 25 centimetres long. We do not retain the unusable ends.

Can we accommodate one extra learner and still keep a demonstration piece under our reuse rule? Work through three options: keep the existing remainder, cut one additional practice strip, or divide the remainder into two equal pieces. Explain which goals each option meets, then write a short, realistic teacher–volunteer discussion resolving the tradeoff.

- **Keep the existing remainder:** Cut eight strips and retain the single 40 cm piece. This serves the original eight learners and meets the demonstration rule, but the extra learner has no strip.
- **Cut one additional strip:** Nine strips need 315 cm. From 320 cm usable, 5 cm remains. The extra learner gets a strip, but the remainder is scrap because it is shorter than 25 cm.
- **Divide the existing remainder equally:** The 40 cm piece becomes two 20 cm pieces. Neither meets the retention threshold, and neither supplies a 35 cm strip. This meets neither additional goal.

**Teacher:** We can keep the 40 cm piece for the demonstration, or cut a ninth strip and have only 5 cm left.

**Volunteer:** The ninth learner needs practice too. Could we use separate material for the demonstration?

**Teacher:** If we can find some, let’s cut the ninth strip and classify the 5 cm as scrap. Otherwise, we’ll need to choose between the extra strip and keeping this demonstration piece.

For a future class, change the demonstration reuse rule so that pieces can qualify by their combined length; practice strips must still be cut as before. Reassess all three options we discussed using the earlier measurements and threshold. Can we accommodate the extra learner and meet the revised demonstration rule in each case?

- **Keep the 40 cm remainder:** The original eight learners get strips, and the 40 cm available for the demonstration exceeds the 25 cm combined-length threshold. The extra learner does not get a strip.
- **Cut a ninth strip:** Nine strips use 315 cm of the 320 cm usable section, leaving 5 cm. All nine learners get strips, but the remainder falls short of the 25 cm demonstration threshold.
- **Divide the 40 cm remainder equally:** Two 20 cm pieces have a combined length of 40 cm, so together they qualify under the revised rule. They do not provide a 35 cm practice strip, so the extra learner remains unaccommodated.

The revised rule allows the two 20 cm pieces to qualify together, but none of these options meets both goals. The unusable ends are excluded throughout.

I'm learning about a fictional offline task queue. What does this trace establish, and what remains unknown? Does my explanation follow?

Task T7: send a confirmation to a simulated external service.
10:00:00 worker A receives T7, delivery 1.
10:00:01 service records an effect for request key K7.
10:00:02 worker A records SUCCESS locally.
10:00:03 worker A crashes.
10:00:30 queue redelivers T7 to worker B, delivery 2.
10:00:31 worker B sends K7 again.
10:00:32 service records another effect for K7.

My explanation: “Because the worker recorded success, the queue must have acknowledged delivery, so the second effect proves the queue lost a message.”

The trace shows two deliveries and two recorded service effects for the same request key. A local success record did not prevent the second delivery or effect.

Your explanation does not follow: local success and queue acknowledgement may be separate events, and the trace shows no acknowledgement. It also does not establish that the queue lost a message; it shows a redelivery. The reason for that redelivery, the queue’s acknowledgement rules, and whether the service was supposed to deduplicate K7 remain unknown.
The worker sends the queue acknowledgement only after recording local success, and A crashed before sending it. What does that tell us about the redelivery and at-least-once delivery?

- A crashed before acknowledging T7, so redelivery is consistent with a queue retrying an unacknowledged delivery. It does not show that a message was lost.
- This illustrates why at-least-once delivery can produce duplicate processing: the service effect happened before the acknowledgement, and the retry produced another effect.
- The trace alone does not establish the queue’s delivery guarantee or the exact cause of redelivery. A service-side idempotency rule for K7 could prevent duplicate effects, but the trace shows no effective deduplication here.

Add this to the trace: at 10:00:33, while B is still active, the queue delivers a separate copy of T7 to worker C as delivery 3. C sends K7 at 10:00:34, and the service records a third effect at 10:00:35. What does this add to the explanation?

The new events show that duplicate processing can overlap: B and C were both active on separate deliveries of T7, and each produced an effect for K7. A retry does not necessarily wait for an earlier worker to finish.

The trace still does not establish why C received its copy or the queue’s overall delivery guarantee. Preventing duplicate effects would require coordination that works for concurrent requests, such as atomic service-side idempotency for K7; checking for an earlier effect without an atomic claim could race.
Is retrying the same thing as making the operation idempotent? Would including K7 in every request by itself prevent the three effects, including when B and C overlap?

No. Retrying repeats an attempt; idempotency ensures repeated attempts have the same effect as one attempt. Including K7 in each request supplies a key, but does not prevent duplicates by itself. The service must enforce idempotency for that key, including atomically coordinating concurrent requests so B and C cannot both create an effect. The trace shows three effects, so including K7 did not prevent them here.

One clarification: A’s local SUCCESS only records that the worker received a response; it is not independent verification that an effect occurred. What do the service’s separate records establish, and what remains uncertain?

The service’s separate records show three recorded effects for K7, one after each worker’s request. A’s local SUCCESS independently establishes only that A received a response; it does not verify an effect.

The trace does not establish why C received another delivery, the queue’s overall delivery guarantee, or whether the service was intended to deduplicate K7. It also does not independently establish anything beyond what the service records report about those effects.

Could you show two worked alternative traces from the same starting point: one where the service allows duplicate effects and one where it atomically deduplicates K7? Include acknowledgement timing and overlapping deliveries in both.

Starting from A’s first delivery in both examples:

**Service allows duplicates**
1. A receives T7, sends K7, and the service records effect 1.
2. A receives a response and records SUCCESS locally, then crashes before acknowledging the queue.
3. The queue redelivers T7 to B. B sends K7; the service records effect 2.
4. While B is still active and before B acknowledges, the queue delivers another copy to C. C sends K7; the service records effect 3.
5. B and C each acknowledge their deliveries after completing their work. Those acknowledgements do not undo the three effects.

**Service atomically deduplicates K7**
1. A receives T7, sends K7, and the service atomically records effect 1 and K7’s completed result.
2. A receives a response and records SUCCESS locally, then crashes before acknowledging.
3. The queue redelivers T7 to B. B sends K7; the service recognizes the completed key and returns the stored result without another effect.
4. While B is still active and before B acknowledges, C receives another copy and sends K7. The same atomic rule returns the stored result without another effect.
5. B and C acknowledge their deliveries after receiving the result. There is one service effect despite three deliveries.

These are illustrative traces: the original trace does not establish why C received its copy. Atomic coordination also matters if B and C reach the service simultaneously before either request has completed.

I no longer want the deployment checklist I was considering; let’s keep this conceptual. What if the service applies the effect but its response is lost, so the worker cannot tell whether it happened? Explain the consequences for retrying and verification.

The worker has an ambiguous outcome: a lost response cannot tell it whether the service applied the effect. Retrying may complete an operation that never happened, but may also create a second effect if it did.

A stable key such as K7 helps only if the service atomically enforces idempotency for it. Then the worker can retry with the same key and obtain the existing result without repeating the effect, including during overlapping attempts.

Alternatively, the worker can query a reliable service record for K7 before deciding what to do. A missing record is conclusive only if that lookup is authoritative and sufficiently current; a stale or incomplete lookup could lead to another duplicate. A local record of a response alone would not independently verify the effect.

Could you turn this into a realistic teaching dialogue? Have the learner revisit the original explanation, the overlapping deliveries, and the lost-response case, while distinguishing the worker's local record from the service's evidence.

**Learner:** A recorded SUCCESS, so the queue must have acknowledged the task. Does the retry prove it lost a message?

**Guide:** No. We now know A crashed before sending the queue acknowledgement. Its local SUCCESS only says it received a response. The service’s separate records report an effect for K7; the local record does not independently verify that effect. Redelivery is consistent with retrying an unacknowledged task, not evidence of message loss.

**Learner:** Then B received the retry. Why did C get another copy while B was still active?

**Guide:** The trace doesn’t say why. It does show overlapping deliveries: B and C both sent K7, and the service recorded an effect for each. It doesn’t establish the queue’s overall delivery guarantee.

**Learner:** If both requests carried K7, shouldn’t that have stopped the duplicates?

**Guide:** The key identifies the operation, but the service must enforce idempotency for it. That enforcement must handle concurrent requests atomically, or B and C could both create an effect.

**Learner:** What if the service applies the effect but its response is lost?

**Guide:** The worker cannot tell from the missing response whether the effect happened. A retry could finish an operation that never happened, or duplicate one that did. If the service atomically enforces idempotency, retrying with the same key can return the existing result without another effect.

**Learner:** Could the worker check first instead?

**Guide:** It could query a reliable service record. But a missing entry is conclusive only if the lookup is authoritative and current enough; a stale result could make the worker retry after an effect already occurred.

Suppose we try to deduplicate using only each worker’s local SUCCESS record. Can you walk through two concrete crash or race timelines using the same workers and request key: one with a local marker written before the service call and one with SUCCESS recorded after it? Include overlapping workers and keep the established meaning of SUCCESS precise. Conclude with what service-side guarantees would be needed, without assuming new infrastructure or turning this into a deployment checklist.

**Marker before the service call**

1. A receives T7 and writes a local “started” marker for K7, then crashes before sending the request. That marker cannot be called SUCCESS: no response was received.
2. B and C receive overlapping deliveries. If they treat A’s marker as proof of completion, they may both skip the call even though no effect occurred. If markers are local to each worker, B and C may not see A’s marker at all and may both call the service.

**SUCCESS after the service call**

1. A sends K7. The service applies an effect, but its response is lost; A crashes before recording SUCCESS or acknowledging the queue.
2. B and C receive overlapping deliveries. Neither has evidence from A’s local SUCCESS that the operation completed. Both send K7, and a service without deduplication can record two more effects. Even if A had received a response and recorded SUCCESS, that record would only establish receipt of a response, not independently verify the effect; local records also do not by themselves coordinate concurrent workers.

To prevent duplicate effects, the service needs to enforce a stable key atomically across concurrent requests and couple its deduplication decision with the effect and recoverable result. A retry with K7 can then retrieve the existing result. Alternatively, verification needs an authoritative, sufficiently current service record, with coordination against races between checking and acting. The trace itself does not establish that either guarantee exists.

Suppose B and C each query an authoritative, current shared record for K7 and call the service if the key is absent. Can you show an explicit interleaving that tests whether correct reads eliminate the race? Distinguish observing an absent key from reserving it, and explain where an atomic boundary is needed.

- **Correct reads do not eliminate the race:** observing an absent key does not reserve it. For example:

  1. B queries the authoritative, current shared record for K7 and sees it is absent.
  2. Before B acts, C queries the same record and also sees K7 is absent.
  3. B calls the service with K7; the service applies an effect.
  4. C calls the service with K7; without service-side deduplication, it applies a second effect.

- Both reads were correct when made. The problem is the gap between checking and acting: neither read prevents another worker from making the same decision.
- An atomic reservation can ensure only one worker claims K7, but a reservation alone is insufficient if the claimant crashes before or after the effect. To prevent duplicate effects while supporting recovery, the service needs an atomic boundary coupling the key’s deduplication state with the effect and a recoverable result, including for overlapping requests. The trace does not establish that such a guarantee exists.

Why does this Python CSV adapter fail on the catalogue below? Please identify problems beyond the first exception, using the actual rows as evidence.

```csv
book_id,title,revision
A1,"Map, Moon",1
B2,,2
A1,"Map, Moon Revised",3
C3,Quiet Harbor,not-a-number
A1,Tied Edition,3
```

```python
def read_catalogue(text):
    lines = text.splitlines()
    records = {}
    for line in lines[1:]:
        book_id, title, revision = line.split(',')
        records[book_id] = (title, int(revision))
    return records
```

The first data row fails because splitting on every comma produces four fields: the comma inside "Map, Moon" is part of the quoted title, but `str.split(',')` does not understand CSV quoting.

Other problems appear later in the catalogue:
- `B2,,2` has an empty title. The code accepts it without validation; whether that is allowed depends on the catalogue rules.
- `C3,Quiet Harbor,not-a-number` raises `ValueError` when the revision is converted to an integer.
- `A1` occurs three times. Assigning to `records[book_id]` silently overwrites earlier entries. If parsing and conversion succeeded, `Tied Edition` would overwrite `Map, Moon Revised`, even though both have revision 3. The code neither selects the highest revision explicitly nor defines how to resolve ties.

Use Python’s `csv` module for parsing, then validate fields and define duplicate and tie-handling rules.

The title column is required, but an empty title is valid. A missing required header is a file-level error, and extra columns are acceptable. How does that change your assessment of B2 and the header handling?

- B2 is valid: the title field is present and empty, which your rules allow.
- The current code skips the first line without checking it. It should verify that `book_id`, `title`, and `revision` headers are present and report a file-level error if any are missing. It should also map values by header name so extra columns and column order do not break parsing.

Also, book_id must be nonempty and revision must be a nonnegative integer. Errors should identify the physical CSV row number, counting the header as row 1. Quoted fields can contain commas and newlines. What does that mean for validation and row numbering?

Validate each parsed record by header name: `book_id` must be present and nonempty, `title` must be present but may be empty, and `revision` must be a nonnegative integer. Thus B2 remains valid, while C3 has an invalid revision. A missing required header is a file-level error; extra columns are allowed.

Use `csv.reader` or `csv.DictReader` with a text stream that preserves CSV newline handling. A logical record can span several physical lines, so enumerate records does not give physical row numbers. Track the starting physical line for each record using the reader’s `line_num` after the preceding record; `line_num` after reading the current record gives its ending line. Define which line to report for a multiline record—its starting line is a useful convention—and include the range if helpful.

For duplicate IDs, keep the row with the highest revision; if revisions tie, keep the first occurrence. Every row must be validated, even if it would lose deduplication. How does that affect the original catalogue?

With CSV-aware parsing and validation, B2 on row 3 is valid. For A1, row 4 wins: revision 3 is higher than row 2’s revision 1, and row 6 also has revision 3 but loses the tie because it comes later. Row 5 must still be reported as invalid because `not-a-number` is not a nonnegative integer. Every row must be validated before applying the duplicate rule. Whether valid records are returned alongside errors still needs a defined policy.
Could you walk through the original rows in order, showing validation and how the A1 selection changes, including the invalid revision and the tie? Please hold off on the full parser for now.

Counting the header as row 1:

- Row 2: A1, “Map, Moon”, revision 1 is valid. Select it as the first A1 entry.
- Row 3: B2 has a present but empty title, which is valid; revision 2 is valid. It does not affect A1.
- Row 4: A1, “Map, Moon Revised”, revision 3 is valid. It replaces row 2 because 3 is higher than 1.
- Row 5: C3 has an invalid revision, `not-a-number`. Report the error on physical row 5.
- Row 6: A1, “Tied Edition”, revision 3 is valid. It ties row 4, so row 4 remains selected as the first occurrence at that revision.

The handling of valid records alongside the row 5 error remains unspecified.

Now consider this second file:

```csv
book_id,revision
B2,2
```

How should its missing title header be handled, and how does that differ from B2’s blank title in the original file?

The second file has a file-level error because the required `title` header is missing. Report that error before processing its data rows.

In the original file, the `title` header exists and B2’s title field is present but empty. That row is valid under your rules.

Make the parser all-or-nothing: collect row validation errors and return no catalogue if any exist; header errors stop processing, and CSV syntax errors must also prevent a partial result. How would you use the standard library to handle quoted multiline fields and report each record’s starting physical row? Please propose a clear return or exception contract, but hold off on the full parser.

Use `csv.reader` with a text stream opened using `newline=''` and `strict=True`. Read and validate the header first: if a required name is missing, return a file-level error without processing data rows. Map columns by name and allow extras.

Track physical lines supplied to the reader. For each logical record, report the first physical line belonging to it; a quoted field can span multiple lines, and `reader.line_num` after reading gives the ending line. Account for blank lines that the reader skips when identifying the start.

For each record, validate the required fields before considering deduplication. Collect row errors while continuing through parseable records. Among valid rows with the same ID, retain the highest revision and keep the first on a tie.

Contract: `read_catalogue` returns `(catalogue, errors)`. On success, `errors` is empty; on any error, `catalogue` is `None`. Header and CSV syntax errors stop parsing; row errors are collected through all parseable records. Error row numbers are starting physical lines. Revisions use ASCII decimal digits, subject to the configured `csv.field_size_limit`; chunk conversion avoids Python's integer-string conversion limit.

```python
import csv
import io
import unittest


def decimal_value(s):
    # Small chunks avoid Python's integer-string conversion limit locally.
    value = 0
    for i in range(0, len(s), 9):
        chunk = s[i:i + 9]
        value = value * (10 ** len(chunk)) + int(chunk)
    return value


def read_catalogue(text):
    reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(text, newline=''), strict=True)
    required = ('book_id', 'title', 'revision')
    errors = []
    records = {}
    start = 1
    try:
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header is None or any(name not in header for name in required):
            return None, ['Missing required header']
        # Ambiguous required columns cannot be mapped reliably.
        if any(header.count(name) != 1 for name in required):
            return None, ['Duplicate required header']
        indices = {name: header.index(name) for name in required}
        while True:
            start = reader.line_num + 1
            try:
                row = next(reader)
            except StopIteration:
                break
            if not row:  # Blank physical line; the next record starts later.
                continue
            missing = [name for name, i in indices.items() if i >= len(row)]
            if missing:
                errors.append(f'Row {start}: missing fields: {", ".join(missing)}')
                continue
            book_id, title, revision = (row[indices[n]] for n in required)
            problems = []
            if not book_id:
                problems.append('empty book_id')
            if not revision or any(c < '0' or c > '9' for c in revision):
                problems.append('invalid revision')
            if problems:
                errors.append(f'Row {start}: {", ".join(problems)}')
                continue
            rev = decimal_value(revision)
            if book_id not in records or rev > records[book_id][1]:
                records[book_id] = (title, rev)
    except csv.Error as exc:
        errors.append(f'CSV syntax error starting at physical row {start}: {exc}')
    return (None, errors) if errors else (records, [])


class CatalogueTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_original_all_or_nothing(self):
        text = ('book_id,title,revision\nA1,"Map, Moon",1\nB2,,2\n'
                'A1,"Map, Moon Revised",3\nC3,Quiet Harbor,not-a-number\n'
                'A1,Tied Edition,3\n')
        result, errors = read_catalogue(text)
        self.assertIsNone(result)
        self.assertEqual(len(errors), 1)
        self.assertIn('Row 5', errors[0])

    def test_header_and_blank_title(self):
        self.assertIsNone(read_catalogue('book_id,revision\nB2,2\n')[0])
        self.assertEqual(read_catalogue('book_id,title,revision\nB2,,2\n'),
                         ({'B2': ('', 2)}, []))

    def test_duplicates_and_extra_columns(self):
        text = ('revision,extra,title,book_id\n1,x,Old,A\n3,x,Winner,A\n'
                '3,x,Tie,A\n2,x,Later,A\n')
        self.assertEqual(read_catalogue(text), ({'A': ('Winner', 3)}, []))

    def test_multiline_start_and_multiple_errors(self):
        text = ('book_id,title,revision\n\nA,"two\nlines",bad\n'
                'B,ok,-1\n')
        result, errors = read_catalogue(text)
        self.assertIsNone(result)
        self.assertEqual(len(errors), 2)
        self.assertIn('Row 3', errors[0])
        self.assertIn('Row 5', errors[1])

    def test_malformed_csv(self):
        result, errors = read_catalogue('book_id,title,revision\nA,good,1\nB,"unfinished\nrecord')
        self.assertIsNone(result)
        self.assertTrue(any('CSV syntax error starting at physical row 3' in e for e in errors))

    def test_long_revision_then_invalid_row(self):
        digits = '9' * 4500
        result, errors = read_catalogue(
            'book_id,title,revision\nA,long,' + digits + '\nB,bad,no\n')
        self.assertIsNone(result)
        self.assertEqual(len(errors), 1)
        self.assertIn('Row 3', errors[0])
        result, errors = read_catalogue('book_id,title,revision\nA,long,' + digits + '\n')
        self.assertEqual(errors, [])
        self.assertEqual(result['A'][1], 10 ** 4500 - 1)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

```python
class Buffer:
    def __init__(self, text=''):
        if not isinstance(text, str):
            raise TypeError('text must be a string')
        self.text = text
        self.cursor = len(text)
        self.undo_stack = []
        self.redo_stack = []

    def _edit(self, text, cursor):
        self.undo_stack.append((self.text, self.cursor))
        self.redo_stack.clear()
        self.text, self.cursor = text, cursor

    def insert(self, s):
        if not isinstance(s, str):
            raise TypeError('insertion must be a string')
        if s:
            p = self.cursor
            self._edit(self.text[:p] + s + self.text[p:], p + len(s))

    def delete(self, count):
        if type(count) is not int:
            raise TypeError('count must be an integer')
        if count < 0 or count > len(self.text) - self.cursor:
            raise ValueError('deletion out of bounds')
        if count:
            p = self.cursor
            self._edit(self.text[:p] + self.text[p + count:], p)
```
